passage: Note, Arnab, class teacher. Lopa read me a line from the letter she wrote to her grandmother, who died in January. On her grandmother's birthday, Lopa told me, the family lit a lamp on the balcony, and she cooked her grandmother's favourite khichdi with her mother and cousins, following a recipe in her grandmother's handwriting. She said the kitchen smelled like Nani's kitchen, and everyone laughed and cried in the same minute. She plans to do it every year. I asked whether she would like me to keep an eye on her school workload in April. She said she was fine, and thanked me. I will check in quietly, and I'm glad she has found her own way of staying close to her grandmother.

qa.q: What dish did Lopa cook on her grandmother's birthday?
qa.a: Lopa cooked her grandmother's favourite khichdi.

qa.q: What was Lopa feeling when everyone laughed and cried in the same minute?
qa.a: Lopa was feeling bittersweet, sad and comforted together, since the kitchen smelled like Nani's kitchen.

qa.q: What else could Lopa add to her remembrance?
qa.a: Lopa could keep writing letters or look at photos or visit a place her grandmother loved, since more small rituals give the bond a lasting home.

qa.q: How might Lopa's mother see the day?
qa.a: Lopa's mother probably feels comforted to share the memory with her family, since they cooked, laughed and cried together.

grounding: A teen writes a letter to her grandmother, lights a lamp on her birthday and cooks her favourite dish with the family, keeping the bond alive.
